title: What Happens When One Jammed Slide Revealed Edge Detectors?
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Hubel & Wiesel (1959): How a Jammed Glass Slide Accidentally Cracked the Visual Cortex's Edge Code, grounded in D. H. Hubel, T. N. Wiesel (1959) (The Journal of Physiology). Empirical findings show that in 1958 in a cramped basement room at Johns Hopkins's Wilmer Institute, two young postdocs — David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel — lowered a tungsten microelectrode (invented by Hubel) beside a single neuron in primary visual cortex (V1) wired to an audio loudspeaker that clicked 'pop-pop' whenever the cell fired.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how retina, primary visual cortex, temporal lobe coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that because their mentor Stephen Kuffler had just proved retinal cells love tiny round spots of light (center-surround doughnuts), Hubel & Wiesel spent hours shining bright spots, dark spots, and full-room flashes onto the screen — and the stubborn V1 cortical neuron stayed stone-cold silent.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- D. H. Hubel, T. N. Wiesel (1959). Receptive fields of single neurones in the cat's striate cortex. The Journal of Physiology. https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.1959.sp006308
- David Hubel, Torsten Wiesel (2012). David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2012.07.002
- Torsten N. Wiesel, David H. Hubel (1963). Single-Cell Responses in Striate Cortex of Kittens Deprived of Vision in One Eye. Journal of Neurophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.1963.26.6.1003
